blocks.label: SUPPLEMENTAL:
blocks.text: This guide covers the whole course and is **not** the Quiz 1 guide. For the upcoming quiz, use the Quiz 1 Study Guide.
Programming versus learning

rows: Data **and rules** written by a person

blocks.text: Example: converting miles to kilometres. A programmer would type the rule. A learning algorithm is shown many (miles, km) pairs and finds the rule itself, a line **y = m*x + b** with m close to 1.6 and b close to 0. m and b are the **parameters** that training finds.
Correlation

rows: Strong positive relationship: both rise together
Strong negative (inverse) relationship: one rises as the other falls

blocks.text: Regression models

items: **Linear regression:** one input, y = mx + b; a simple form of predictive analytics.
**Multivariate regression:** two or more inputs, each with its own coefficient; training finds the best coefficients.
**Logistic regression:** produces a probability that is compared with a threshold (such as 0.5); used for **binary classification**.

blocks.text: Deep learning
Machine learning with **neural networks that have 2 or more hidden layers**. The output of one layer is the input of the next.

Supervised learning learns a mapping from inputs to **labels** (the correct answers). The data is split into a **training set (about 70-80%)** and a **test set (about 20-30%)**. Both must contain inputs and correct labels. The trained model is then used on **new** data.

rows: Vote among the labels of the k nearest training points
k is a hyperparameter; small k overfits, large k underfits
Questions about feature values lead down the tree to a class
Traditional ML needed hand-picked features (salary, commute...)
Finds a boundary between classes using the **support vectors**
Good in high dimensions; memory efficient; kernel functions; no direct probabilities

blocks.text: Linear separability
Classes are **linearly separable** when a straight line (or flat plane) can split one from the other.
Datasets used in class

items: **Iris:** 150 flowers, 3 labels (setosa, versicolor, virginica), 4 features in cm (sepal length and width, petal length and width).
**Spam:** 57 input columns (word and character frequencies, capital-letter run lengths) and a 58th column, the label: 1 = spam, 0 = not spam.

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: Classification has a discrete target; regression has a continuous one. Logistic regression is classification despite its name.

rows: Grid of actual versus predicted classes: **TP**, **FP**, **FN**, **TN**. It holds as many items as the test set.
Split the data into k folds; each fold is the test set once; k models are scored. With 5 folds, each round is 80% train / 20% test.
How well the model does on examples it never saw

blocks.text: Overfitting and underfitting

rows: Memorizes the training set (and its noise)

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: Positive and negative refer to the class being counted: a **false negative** is an actual positive that the model called negative.
**Clustering** groups similar items without labels. It is **unsupervised**: it does not use a labelled training set. (**Data association** is another unsupervised solution.)

rows: Connect points step by step into a tree of clusters
DBSCAN (density-based spatial clustering of applications with noise)
Group points that are densely packed

blocks.text: Distance between points

rows: Straight-line distance, the hypotenuse; more precise
Sum of horizontal and vertical steps, like walking a city grid; cheaper to compute but less precise

blocks.text: Example: 3 blocks east and 4 north is Manhattan **7** and Euclidean **5**.

rows: **Transform** it: scikit-learn needs numbers, so non-numeric data is converted
**Predict** on live data the model has not seen
**Monitor** the live model; tune, retrain or redeploy if needed

blocks.text: The scikit-learn pattern

x_train, x_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(x, y, test_size=0.2)
model.fit(x_train, y_train)          # train
predictions = model.predict(x_test)  # predict
accuracy_score(y_test, predictions)  # compare with the real labels
With 150 rows and test_size=0.2, that is 120 training rows and 30 test rows.

Feature engineering covers selecting and reducing features, encoding, scaling and regularization. **Feature selection** removes inputs that do not help, which saves time and memory and often improves results.

rows: Scores features by their own characteristics, no model (variance, correlation, SelectKBest)
Trains a model on feature subsets and scores them (forward selection, backward elimination, exhaustive search, **RFE**)
Selection happens while the model is built (**LASSO**); the model is fitted only once

items: **Univariate filter:** a feature with very **low variance** adds little to predicting the target.
**Multivariate filter:** pairwise correlations between features (a correlation heatmap).
**SelectKBest:** keeps the K highest-scoring features (a filter).
**RFE:** repeatedly builds models and drops the weakest feature; features are ranked by the order they were eliminated.

blocks.text: **Dimensions = features = inputs.** Reducing them cuts processing time and RAM and can show which features matter. A column that has no effect on the output can simply be dropped.
Example: if LD1 separates two classes cleanly and LD2 does not, drop LD2 and still get the same results.

rows: Continuous value to **two classes** at a threshold
Views of 5,000 or more = popular, otherwise unpopular
Text categories to **binary columns**, one per category

blocks.label: Why not 1, 2, 3?
blocks.text: Numbering categories implies an **order** (blue > green > red) that does not exist. One-hot avoids that.

items: In pandas: **pd.get_dummies(column)** one-hot encodes a column.
The course slides name scikit-learn's LabelEncoder here. Be aware that it maps categories to integer codes; OneHotEncoder is the class that produces binary columns.

The slides also show a 'multiple-hot' style that writes each category's number in binary and uses one column per bit, which needs fewer columns than one-hot. (Elsewhere, 'multi-hot' can mean a row with several 1s. Use your instructor's wording.)

blocks.text: Attributes may use different scales (a 1-5 rating next to a 1-10 rating). Aligning them improves many ML operations, especially **distance-based** ones such as kNN, where a large-valued feature would dominate.

rows: Distribution unknown or **not Gaussian**; kNN, neural nets

blocks.text: Worked example: min 10, max 110, value 35 gives (35-10)/100 = **0.25**. Mean 60, std dev 5, value 70 gives (70-60)/5 = **2**.
An overfit model tries too hard to capture **noise** and outliers. **Regularization** punishes large weights (coefficients), balancing bias and variance.

rows: Can push coefficients to **exactly zero**, eliminating features
Shrinks weights but **keeps most or all** features
Also acts as embedded feature selection
Smooths out the effect of outliers

blocks.label: Remember:
blocks.text: LASSO = L1. If a model scores 99% on training and 72% on test, regularization, feature selection, more data or a larger k (for kNN) can all help.
